solutions.check: 30 entries; each light the paper's grid did not give solved here from its clue's wordplay (an anagram or hidden word, the one listed word fitting every crossing) and its definition (WordNet), as the answer another puzzle gave the same clue, or as the one past answer its crossings left that the printed letters allow, agrees with the 28 answers the paper printed; printed-crossing fills: 18-across, 29-across

parts.note: a typeface set apart from ordinary roman, the sloping letters printers use to stress a word

explanation.surface: Someone is described, with stress, as quite a different sort of person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type' reads as a kind of person, but it is printing type: the sloping face used when a word is emphasised.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloping print is the standard way of marking emphasis on a word, and it is a separate face from upright roman.

indicators.note: building suggests the letters of street are being put together into a new structure

explanation.surface: Money is to be made from putting up houses along a road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Street-building' looks like construction work, but 'building' is the anagram signal acting on the street, and 'in' is taken as it stands, ahead of the shuffled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Money earned on a loan or deposit is a return, a form of gain.

parts.note: awake because an alarm clock has gone off, or stirred up by fear

explanation.surface: Someone is aware of a sense of fear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conscious of' reads as 'aware of', but it means awake because of: the alarm is a clock that wakes the sleeper.
explanation.definitionFit: Woken from sleep, as by an alarm clock, someone is stirred into consciousness.

clue.text: Staying in, here in the tavern above the church

indicators.note: in a down clue, above means this comes before the next piece
in here means the word here sits inside the word for a tavern

parts.note: an inn is a tavern
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone stays in, here at the pub above the church.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the opening 'Staying in', so the second 'in' does the container work; in a down answer 'above' means 'placed before'. CE stands for the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality of abiding within something as part of its nature is a philosopher's term for remaining within.

definitions.meaning: allotted means handed out as a share or task
a subscription is a signature written underneath, so this reads '...', as the signature says

explanation.surface: Shares or seats were handed out in line with who had paid a subscription.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subscription' looks like a paid membership, but its older sense is a name written beneath a document; split the answer as AS SIGNED.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot something is to give it out as someone's portion; split in two, the letters say 'as signed', matching a signature.

clue.text: Copper given a coat at Yorkshire horse-race ?

definitions.meaning: copper coated with a thin layer of silver, an old technique for tableware
Sheffield is a Yorkshire city, and a plate is a horse race with a trophy as prize

explanation.surface: A police officer is presented with a coat at a race meeting in Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman but is the metal; Sheffield, a Yorkshire city, developed silver plating on copper, and a race for a trophy is a plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper fused with a silver layer was made in Sheffield, and a race named for a Sheffield trophy would carry the same name.

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
Deal is a seaside town in Kent

explanation.surface: A particular seaside town in Kent is said to be flawless.
explanation.walkthrough: Deal is a seaside town on the Kent coast in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Something perfect is the best that could be imagined, a model of excellence.

parts.note: not celebrating an anniversary but being born on this very day

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone is celebrating an anniversary of their birth.
explanation.walkthrough: A birthday usually means an anniversary, but here it is the actual day of birth.
explanation.definitionFit: An infant only just delivered is having its very first birth day.

parts.note: a don is a university teacher
ate means swallowed food

explanation.surface: A teacher gulped down a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' reads as a noun, a gift, but it is the verb, to give.
explanation.definitionFit: To present something is to give it, and to give to a cause is to contribute.

parts.note: H. G. Wells wrote The Time Machine and The War of the Worlds, stories set in imagined futures

explanation.surface: A forward-looking project coming out of the cathedral city of Wells.
explanation.walkthrough: Wells could be the Somerset cathedral city, but it is H. G. Wells, author of The Time Machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Wells's novels of time travel and alien invasion are founding examples of the futuristic genre.

clue.text: To cheat oh, is that perhaps hurtful ?

definitions.text: To cheat oh, is that perhaps hurtful

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters of the opening words could be laid out another way

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether cheating would be a painful thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges TO, CHEAT and OH; the whole clue then describes the result, a pain that certainly hurts.
explanation.definitionFit: A pain in a tooth is a classic hurtful complaint, which the question form of the clue invites.

clue.text: Sainted king would, vulgarly, be victorious

parts.note: would shortened to 'd, spelt out in casual or dialect speech as ED
to be victorious is to win

explanation.surface: A holy monarch, speaking roughly, says he would come out on top.
explanation.walkthrough: St Edwin was a seventh-century king of Northumbria, venerated as a saint.
explanation.definitionFit: Edwin of Northumbria was an Anglo-Saxon monarch later honoured as a saint and martyr.

clue.text: Keep back to give a second helping

definitions.meaning: to keep back is to hold something in hand for later

explanation.surface: A host holds some food back so they can offer seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word as RE (again) and SERVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Holding something back for later is the verb's ordinary sense; serving a plate again is the same letters read as 'serve again'.

clue.text: In nuclear war it won't agree with us

definitions.text: In nuclear war it won't agree with us

parts.words: In nuclear war it won't agree with us
parts.note: the radioactive dust after a nuclear blast harms our health; it also reads as two parties quarrelling

explanation.surface: A grim remark that atomic warfare would disagree with humanity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Won't agree with us' is used as food disagreeing with the stomach, and the answer split as FALL OUT means to quarrel, not agree.
explanation.definitionFit: Radioactive particles that settle after a nuclear explosion poison people, and 'fall out' also means to quarrel.

parts.note: Tyre was a Phoenician port; its great trading rival was a neighbouring Phoenician city

explanation.surface: A rival firm making tyres for cars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tyre' suggests rubber for wheels, but it is the ancient Phoenician city in Lebanon; its rival up the coast was Sidon.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidon and Tyre were the two leading Phoenician cities, rivals in trade along the Lebanese coast.

clue.text: Where such a banking house might be, in a wood ?

definitions.text: Where such a banking house might be, in a wood

parts.words: Where such a banking house might be, in a wood
parts.note: an open space among trees is where a house might stand

explanation.surface: Wondering where a bank's headquarters might be built, perhaps in a forest.
explanation.walkthrough: A clearing house is the office where banks settle cheques between them; a gap in a wood is also called by the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An open patch among trees carries this name, and banks settle cheques through a clearing house.

clue.text: In Sussex, no water for ducks ?

definitions.text: In Sussex, no water for ducks

parts.words: In Sussex, no water for ducks
parts.note: a river in Sussex; read as A RUN, it is what a batsman out for a duck in cricket never scores

explanation.surface: A complaint that ducks in Sussex have nowhere to swim.
explanation.walkthrough: The Arun is a river in Sussex; in cricket a batsman out for 0 has made a 'duck', not even a run, so this water is no place for ducks.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arun flows through West Sussex to the sea, and its name splits as 'a run', which a duck in cricket lacks.

parts.note: to call someone something is to describe them so
an ower is one who owes, a debtor

explanation.surface: Someone is labelled a debtor for being naive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As' is a link joining the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A callow youth is green and untried, so this comparative means more raw.

clue.text: Sails thus fully extended when clear of rocks

definitions.meaning: a reef is a fold taken in a sail to shorten it; with none taken in, the canvas is spread to its full extent
reefs are rocky ridges under the sea, so a stretch with none is free of them

explanation.surface: A yacht spreads all its canvas once it is safely past the rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses use 'reef': a tuck taken in a sail, and an underwater ridge of rock; 'when' is a link between the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: With no reefs (tucks) taken in, sails are spread fully; with no reefs (rocky ridges) about, the water is clear.

parts.note: in skittles the 'cheese' is the heavy disc thrown at the pins standing in the alley

explanation.surface: A stain left by cheese on the ground of a back lane.
explanation.walkthrough: In skittles, a pub game, the thrown disc is called a cheese, and its targets are pins set in an alley, nine of them.
explanation.definitionFit: In the game of skittles, each of the nine wooden targets in the alley is a pin aimed at.

clue.text: Where a Roman might house footballers ?

definitions.meaning: a Roman country house with its estate
Aston ..., the Birmingham football club, is often called by its second word alone

explanation.surface: Asking where a Roman would put up a football team.
explanation.walkthrough: Aston Villa is an English football club from Birmingham, commonly shortened to its second word.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman country estate was a villa, and Aston Villa's players are known by that word.

parts.note: a thrashing; also the act of ... a newborn cub into form, as a bear was said to do

explanation.surface: Someone is knocked into shape by a beating.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer means a thrashing, and 'licking into shape' is the old idea that a mother bear forms her cub by licking it.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrashing is a beating, and the idiom about bears forming cubs uses the same word.

definitions.meaning: James Agate was a famous theatre critic; Jacobean here means belonging to someone named James

explanation.surface: Gemstones once owned by a drama critic of King James's era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jacobean' suggests King James I's time, but means 'of James': James Agate was a leading London drama critic of the 1920s to 1940s, and his possessions are Agate's.
explanation.definitionFit: Banded chalcedony gems carry this name, and the possessive of critic James Agate is spelt identically.

clue.text: Information by red explorer is applicable to class members

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
Eric the Red, the Norse explorer who settled Greenland

explanation.surface: News from a communist traveller applies to people of a certain social class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red' looks political but names Eric the Red, the Viking who founded the Greenland settlements.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that covers every member of a group or kind, rather than one particular, is general to the class.

definitions.meaning: spools of cinema film, the sections a movie is wound on
lively Scottish dances for couples or sets

explanation.surface: Sections of a movie made for a troupe of dancers.
explanation.definitionFit: Spools of film and lively Scottish dances both carry this name.

clue.text: I see, I hear! Rally round anyway for ballads

indicators.note: round means the jumbled letters of the rally word go about the other piece
anyway, in any old order, tells us the word rally is to be scrambled
I hear says the phrase I see is taken as it sounds, two letter names

parts.note: said out loud, I see sounds like the letters I and C

explanation.surface: An exclamation of understanding, then a call to gather round for some songs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I hear' turns I SEE into the letter names I C; 'anyway' scrambles RALLY to LYRAL, which goes 'round' them: LYR-IC-AL.
explanation.definitionFit: Words fit to be sung, like those of songs, are described as songlike in style.

parts.note: a Native American dwelling of poles and skins, built with no stone, and no Freemasons' lodge either

explanation.surface: A Masonic lodge in India that has nothing to do with Freemasonry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lodge' and 'masonry' suggest the Freemasons, but the lodge is a conical tent of skins, built with no stonework.
explanation.definitionFit: Plains peoples of North America lived in conical tents of hides on poles, made without any stone.

clue.text: Get underground opinion of TV meeting

parts.note: to inter is to bury, putting a body underground
a view is an opinion

explanation.surface: Finding out what the Tube's passengers think of a television programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underground' suggests the London Tube, but to inter is to bury.
explanation.definitionFit: A televised session where a presenter questions a guest is a formal question-and-answer meeting.

clue.text: Did Jack Point do so in such a voice?

definitions.text: Did Jack Point do so in such a voice?

parts.words: Did Jack Point do so in such a voice?
parts.note: Jack Point, jester in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera The Yeomen of the Guard, sings 'I have a song to sing, O'

explanation.surface: Asking whether a theatrical jester spoke in a particular tone.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Point is the jester in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Yeomen of the Guard, whose duet begins 'I have a song to sing, O'; he did sing a song, in a lilting voice.
explanation.definitionFit: A lilting, rising-and-falling way of speaking is called by this name, and split it says he sang a song.

indicators.note: from here means the letters are made out of the word orange, rebuilt into a new word

explanation.surface: Pointing at a donkey that has come from the Dutch house of Orange or the French town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' signals that ORANGE is rearranged; 'That' is a link pointing at the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The onager is a wild donkey of Asia, a species of wild equid.
